section.title: The Portions for the Priests
section.sectionRationale: This chapter closes the entire first collection of sacrificial law. It gives the law of the guilt offering, adds detailed rules for the peace offering's thanksgiving, vow, and freewill forms, forbids eating fat or blood, and finally states what belongs to the priests, closing with a summary of all five offerings given at Sinai.
section.thesis: God closes the sacrificial law by detailing the guilt offering's procedure, the timing rules for eating the peace offering, the permanent ban on eating fat and blood, and the priestly portions, the breast and thigh, teaching that those who serve at the altar are rightly provided for by the people they serve.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the law of the guilt offering; the law of the peace offering and its timing for thanksgiving, vow, and freewill forms; the ban on fat and blood; and the priestly portions with the chapter's closing summary.

units.label: The law of the guilt offering
units.note: most holy, belonging to the priest

verses.text: “Now this is the law of the guilt offering, which is most holy:
The guilt offering must be slaughtered in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, and the priest shall sprinkle its blood on all sides of the altar.
And all the fat from it shall be offered: the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which is to be removed with the kidneys.
The priest shall burn them on the altar as an offering made by fire to the LORD; it is a guilt offering.
Every male among the priests may eat of it. It must be eaten in a holy place; it is most holy.
The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both. It belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it.
As for the priest who presents a burnt offering for anyone, the hide of that offering belongs to him.
Likewise, every grain offering that is baked in an oven or cooked in a pan or on a griddle belongs to the priest who presents it,
and every grain offering, whether dry or mixed with oil, belongs equally to all the sons of Aaron.

units.label: The law of the peace offering

verses.text: Now this is the law of the peace offering that one may present to the LORD:

If he offers it in {{todah|thanksgiving}}, then along with the sacrifice of thanksgiving he shall offer unleavened cakes mixed with olive oil, unleavened wafers coated with oil, and well-kneaded cakes of fine flour mixed with oil.
Along with his peace offering of thanksgiving he is to present an offering with cakes of leavened bread.
From the cakes he must present one portion of each offering as a contribution to the LORD. It belongs to the priest who sprinkles the blood of the peace offering.
The meat of the sacrifice of his peace offering of thanksgiving must be eaten on the day he offers it; none of it may be left until morning.
If, however, the sacrifice he offers is a vow or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day he presents his sacrifice, but the remainder may be eaten on the next day.
But any meat of the sacrifice remaining until the third day must be burned up.

If any of the meat from his peace offering is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted. It will not be credited to the one who presented it; it shall be an abomination, and the one who eats of it shall bear his iniquity.
Meat that touches anything unclean must not be eaten; it is to be burned up. As for any other meat, anyone who is ceremonially clean may eat it.
But if anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people.

If one touches anything unclean, whether human uncleanness, an unclean animal, or any unclean, detestable thing, and then eats any of the meat of the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people.”
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘You are not to eat any of the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat.
The fat of an animal found dead or mauled by wild beasts may be used for any other purpose, but you must not eat it.
If anyone eats the fat of an animal from which an offering made by fire may be presented to the LORD, the one who eats it must be cut off from his people.
You must not eat the blood of any bird or animal in any of your dwellings.
If anyone eats blood, that person must be cut off from his people.’”
Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the Israelites and say, ‘Anyone who presents a peace offering to the LORD must bring it as his sacrifice to the LORD.
With his own hands he is to bring the offerings made by fire to the LORD; he shall bring the fat, together with the breast, and {{tenufah|wave the breast}} as a wave offering before the LORD.
The priest is to burn the fat on the altar, but the breast belongs to Aaron and his sons.
And you are to give the right thigh to the priest as a {{terumah|contribution}} from your peace offering.
The son of Aaron who presents the blood and fat of the peace offering shall have the right thigh as a portion.

I have taken from the sons of Israel the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution of their peace offerings, and I have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as a permanent portion from the sons of Israel.’”
This is the portion of the offerings made by fire to the LORD for Aaron and his sons since the day they were presented to serve the LORD as priests.
On the day they were anointed, the LORD commanded that this be given them by the sons of Israel. It is a permanent portion for the generations to come.
This is the law of the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering, and the peace offering,
which the LORD gave Moses on Mount Sinai on the day He commanded the Israelites to present their offerings to the LORD in the Wilderness of Sinai.

todah.gloss: Thanksgiving, one specific occasion for the peace offering, given in response to a specific answered prayer or deliverance. Its meat had to be eaten the same day, so that gratitude was expressed and shared immediately, not delayed or hoarded.

tenufah.gloss: A wave offering, presented with a horizontal waving motion before the LORD, symbolically presenting the portion to God before it is given to the priest who serves at the altar.

terumah.gloss: A contribution or heave offering, lifted up and set apart as a gift dedicated to the LORD, then given as the rightful, permanent portion of the priests who minister on Israel's behalf.

basic.context: This long chapter closes the entire opening collection of sacrificial law. It details the guilt offering's procedure, adds rules for the peace offering's thanksgiving, vow, and freewill forms, and their strict timing for eating the meat, permanently forbids eating fat or blood, and finally specifies that the breast and thigh of the peace offering belong to the priests who serve at the altar.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes actual old covenant ritual law and priestly provision for Israel; it is not a code Christians observe today. Its abiding truth is that those who serve God's people at the altar deserve to be supported by those they serve, and that gratitude to God, pictured in the thanksgiving offering, calls for prompt, shared celebration rather than delay.
basic.originalLanguages: The todah, thanksgiving offering, had to be eaten the same day, teaching that gratitude is meant to be expressed immediately and shared, not hoarded. The tenufah, wave offering, and terumah, contribution, describe the breast and thigh set apart and lifted up as the priests' permanent portion for their service at the altar.
basic.typology: The requirement that thanksgiving offerings be eaten the same day, shared in community rather than kept back, anticipates the immediate, communal joy of the Lord's Supper, where believers give thanks, eucharisteo, together. The priest's rightful portion from the people's offerings anticipates Paul's teaching that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel, 1 Corinthians 9:14.
basic.christ: Christ is the true and greater priest, whose provision does not come from the people's offerings but who Himself is the offering, giving His body and blood so that His people might partake, echoing the priestly meal that pictured shared fellowship through sacrifice, 1 Corinthians 10:16-17.
basic.god: God ensures that those who mediate atonement, the priests, are provided for by the very people they serve, showing His concern for those in ministry not to be left destitute. He also insists that thanksgiving be expressed promptly and shared, not hoarded privately, revealing His desire for gratitude that spills outward into community.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 9:13-14 argues that those who serve at the altar share in what is offered, just as the Lord commanded those who preach the gospel to receive their living from it. 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 speaks of sharing one bread together as participation in Christ. Hebrews 13:15 calls believers to offer a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name.
basic.oneStory: This closing chapter of the sacrificial law provides for the priests who serve at the altar and calls Israel to prompt, shared thanksgiving rather than delayed or private gratitude. It anticipates the New Testament pattern of supporting gospel ministers and gathering to give thanks together in Christ, our true peace offering, at His table.

context.literary:
Leviticus 7 finishes the priestly manual that began at 6:8, and it keeps the same heading, 'this is the law of,' at 7:1 and 7:11. It has four parts. Verses 1 to 10 give the rite of the guilt offering, which Leviticus 5:14 to 6:7 had described only by its cases, and then add a note on the priests' shares of other offerings. Verses 11 to 21 give the law of the peace offering in its three forms. Verses 22 to 27 turn to all Israel with a ban on eating fat and blood. Verses 28 to 36 set the priests' portion of the peace offering, and verses 37 and 38 close the whole collection of Leviticus 1 to 7.

There is a notable shift in audience. Verses 1 to 21 continue the instruction to the priests, but verses 22 and 28 begin 'Speak to the Israelites.' The two sections on fat, blood and the priests' portion concern every household, because every Israelite could bring a peace offering and eat from it.

The guilt offering section ends with a principle that ties the book's two atoning sacrifices together: 'The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both,' 7:7. The one difference in the rite is the blood, which is sprinkled 'on all sides of the altar,' 7:2, like the burnt and peace offerings, rather than daubed on the horns.

The peace offering section is built around time. The thanksgiving offering must be eaten the same day, 7:15; vow and freewill offerings may last into the next day, 7:16; anything left on the third day is burned, 7:17. It is also built around purity: unclean meat is burned, 7:19, and an unclean person who eats is cut off, 7:20-21.

The closing summary, 7:37-38, lists six laws, including 'the ordination offering,' which has not yet been described in Leviticus. It looks back to Exodus 29 and forward to Leviticus 8, where the priests are ordained. The summary also names the place twice, 'on Mount Sinai' and 'in the Wilderness of Sinai,' anchoring the whole system in the covenant God made there.
context.historical:
For most Israelites meat was not an everyday food. Flocks and herds were capital, kept for wool, milk and breeding. The peace offering was one of the main occasions when an ordinary family ate meat, and it was eaten in God's presence. Elkanah's yearly sacrifice at Shiloh, where 'he would give portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters,' 1 Samuel 1:4, shows such a meal. When Samuel hosted Saul at a sacrificial feast, the cook set before him 'the leg and what was attached to it,' 1 Samuel 9:24, using the word translated 'thigh' in Leviticus 7:32, a portion of honour.

The rule of 7:15 that a thanksgiving offering be eaten the same day had social consequences. A whole animal, with the cakes and loaves of 7:12-13, was far more than one household could eat before morning. The worshiper had to invite others. Proverbs 7:14 turns this into a warning: the seductress says, 'I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows,' meaning she has meat that must be eaten tonight, and she wants company.

The 'fat tail' of 7:3 refers to the broad-tailed sheep of the region, whose tail stored a large mass of fat. It was considered the choicest part and was given to God.

The rules on priestly portions were open to abuse. Eli's sons sent a servant with a three-pronged fork to take whatever it brought up from the pot, and demanded raw meat before the fat had even been burned, 1 Samuel 2:13-16. Their sin was 'severe in the sight of the LORD, for they were treating the LORD's offering with contempt,' 1 Samuel 2:17. Deuteronomy 18:3 names a different set of priestly portions for sacrifices, the shoulder, jowls and stomach, which readers explain in various ways; Leviticus fixes the breast and right thigh for the peace offering at the sanctuary.
context.canonical:
The thanksgiving offering becomes a major theme in the Psalms. 'I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,' Psalm 116:17-18, joins the todah and the vow of 7:12 and 7:16, and places them before a gathered people. Psalm 107:22 calls the rescued to 'offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing.' Psalm 50 turns the offering inward without abolishing it: 'Sacrifice a thank offering to God,' Psalm 50:14, and 'he who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me,' Psalm 50:23. Jeremiah foresees restored Jerusalem filled with 'the voices of those bringing thank offerings,' Jeremiah 33:11. Amos mocks worshipers who make a show of their leavened thank offerings, Amos 4:5.

The ban on blood runs from the covenant with Noah, 'you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it,' Genesis 9:4, through Leviticus 17:10-14, which gives the reason, 'the life of the flesh is in the blood,' to the council of Jerusalem, which asked Gentile believers to abstain 'from blood,' Acts 15:20 and 29. Leviticus 19:5-8 repeats the third day rule with the same warning that the eater 'will bear his iniquity.' Numbers 18:18 confirms the breast and right thigh as the priests'.

In the New Testament Paul argues from these portions that 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings,' 1 Corinthians 9:13, and from the shared sacrificial meal that 'those who eat the sacrifices' are 'fellow partakers in the altar,' 1 Corinthians 10:18. Hebrews 13:15 calls believers to 'offer to God a sacrifice of praise,' language that reflects the thanksgiving offering, and adds sharing with others, Hebrews 13:16.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know that the sacrifices were not only about sin. The peace offering was a celebration: thanks for rescue, the payment of a vow, a spontaneous gift. God wanted His people to eat in His presence and rejoice, and He set the rules so that the joy would be shared with others and the meat would not be hoarded or left to rot.

He also wanted them to see that joy did not cancel holiness. The same passage that invites Israel to feast warns that an unclean person who eats 'must be cut off from his people,' 7:20. Fellowship with God is a gift, but it is fellowship with a holy God.

The ban on fat and blood taught every household that some things belong to God alone. The fat was His portion on the altar, and the blood was the life He had given for atonement, Leviticus 17:11. Even at home, 'in any of your dwellings,' 7:26, Israel was to remember that life is His.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to provide for its priests generously and in an orderly way, so that the men who served at the altar would neither go hungry nor help themselves. God Himself says, 'I have taken … and I have given them to Aaron,' 7:34. The priests' share was a gift from God, not a claim they could enlarge.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The rituals of this chapter were commands for Israel, and they are not binding on the church. Christians do not offer peace offerings, and the timing rules, the priestly portions and the ban on the fat of sacrificial animals belonged to the sanctuary system that Christ has fulfilled, Hebrews 10:1.

The ban on blood is a harder case. It predates Sinai, Genesis 9:4, and Acts 15:29 asks Gentile believers to abstain from it. Many Christians have read that decree as a concession for fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers rather than a permanent food law, in light of Mark 7:19 and Romans 14:14; others keep it as a standing command. Either way, the chapter's reverence for life as God's gift remains.

What carries over clearly is the spirit of the peace offering. Believers are to give thanks 'in every circumstance,' 1 Thessalonians 5:18, to do it together, Colossians 3:15, and to support those who teach them, Galatians 6:6. The shared meal of thanksgiving has its fulfilment at the Lord's table.

debates.question: Why must the thanksgiving peace offering be eaten the same day, while a vow or freewill offering may be eaten over two days, verses 15 to 16?

views.label: Thanksgiving calls for immediate, spontaneous celebration
views.case: A todah offering responds to a specific answered prayer, so its meat is to be consumed quickly, matching the immediacy of the gratitude being expressed, likely requiring the worshiper to gather others quickly to share the meal. Leviticus 22:29-30 repeats the same-day rule for the thank offering.

views.label: A graduated scale distinguishing spontaneous from planned offerings
views.case: Others note that vow and freewill offerings were often planned further in advance, so a longer window for eating them may simply reflect practical differences in how these offerings were normally brought and consumed.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the specific timing rules reinforced eating sacrificial meat while it was fresh and within community, never letting it become an occasion for decay, waste, or careless disregard for what was holy.

debates.question: Does the ban on eating blood, verses 26 to 27, still bind Christians?

views.label: Yes, as a creation ordinance
views.case: The ban was given to Noah, Genesis 9:4, long before Sinai, and so applies to all humanity. The Jerusalem council repeated it for Gentile believers, Acts 15:20 and 29, and did not tie it to the temple. On this view the command stands, grounded in the truth that life belongs to God.

views.label: No, it was fulfilled and then set aside
views.case: Others argue that the ban's reason in Leviticus 17:11 is sacrificial, that blood was reserved for atonement on the altar. Once Christ's blood has made atonement, the reason no longer applies. Mark comments that Jesus' teaching meant 'all foods are clean,' Mark 7:19, and Paul is persuaded 'that nothing is unclean in itself,' Romans 14:14. The Acts decree was a practical guide for table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.

debates.bearing: Christians have held both views in good conscience. The first honours the command's roots before Sinai; the second honours its sacrificial reason and the New Testament's freedom about food. Both agree that the blood of Christ now does what the ban protected, and that life is sacred because it is God's.

debates.question: Was the 'wave offering' actually waved?

views.label: A horizontal motion before the LORD
views.case: The traditional reading takes the verb literally: the priest, with the worshiper's hands under his, moved the breast toward the altar and back, presenting it to God and receiving it back as His gift. Leviticus 8:27 has Moses putting the portions 'in the hands of Aaron and his sons' and waving them.

views.label: A rite of dedication
views.case: Some scholars argue the term describes a ritual of presentation or elevation rather than a particular motion, since the word is also used of the Levites themselves, whom Aaron presents 'as a wave offering,' Numbers 8:11, which hardly involved lifting them.

debates.bearing: The central meaning is the same either way. The portion was first given to God and then given by God to the priest, 7:34. The priest's food came to him as something the LORD had received and then handed on.

study.originalLanguages:
The name of the offering, zevach shelamim, comes from the root of shalom, and the plural form has been read in more than one way: peace offering, fellowship offering, or well-being offering. The Greek Old Testament usually rendered it 'sacrifice of salvation' or deliverance. The range fits the offering's use. It celebrated a restored relationship with God, and it was often brought after a rescue, the occasion of thanksgiving.

The three forms in 7:12-16 are distinct words. Todah, thanksgiving, comes from yadah, to acknowledge or praise. Neder is a vow, something promised to God in a time of need and paid when the prayer was answered; Psalm 116:18 joins it to thanksgiving. Nedavah is a freewill offering, from a root meaning to give willingly; Psalm 54:6 opens with the related adverb, 'Freely I will sacrifice to You.' Gratitude, faithfulness to promises and spontaneous generosity all had their place at the altar.

The warning of 7:18 uses two key terms. Meat eaten on the third day 'will not be credited' to the worshiper, and the verb is chashav, to reckon or count. It is the verb of Genesis 15:6, where Abram's faith 'was credited to him as righteousness,' and of Numbers 18:27, where the Levites' tithe 'will be reckoned to you.' An offering could be counted in the worshiper's favour or not. The same verse calls such meat piggul, 'an abomination,' and Leviticus 19:7 uses the same word, rendered 'tainted.' An offering meant to bring acceptance becomes, if mishandled, something God refuses.

The penalty 'that person must be cut off from his people,' 7:20, 21, 25 and 27, uses the verb karat, to cut. It is also the verb for making a covenant, literally 'cutting' one. The one who despises the covenant meal is cut off from the covenant people. Genesis 17:14 uses the same penalty for the uncircumcised.

The 'ordination offering' of 7:37 is millu'im, 'fillings.' It comes from the Hebrew idiom for installing a priest, to 'fill his hand.' When Exodus 28:41 says 'ordain them,' the Hebrew literally says 'fill their hand,' and Leviticus 8:27 shows the rite: Moses 'put all these in the hands of Aaron and his sons.'

Finally, the fat forbidden in 7:23-25 is chelev, the fat covering and surrounding the organs that belonged to God on the altar, Leviticus 3:3-4 and 3:16. It has traditionally been understood as distinct from the fat within the meat itself, which was not forbidden. The ban was not about diet but about honouring what was set aside for the LORD.

typology.type: The thanksgiving meal eaten together before the LORD, Leviticus 7:12-15
typology.fulfillment: The todah was a sacrifice turned into a feast: bread and meat, shared the same day with others in God's presence. At the Last Supper Jesus 'had given thanks' over the bread and the cup, 1 Corinthians 11:24, and the church gathers at that table 'with gladness,' Acts 2:46. Paul explicitly compares the Supper with Israel's sacrificial meals: 'Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?' 1 Corinthians 10:18. The escalation is that the worshipers now feed on Christ Himself, John 6:55. The type falls short because the meat spoiled by the third day; the life Christ gives does not.

typology.type: The peace offering itself, zevach shelamim, Leviticus 7:11
typology.fulfillment: The peace offering celebrated fellowship with God after sin had been dealt with, which is why it came last in the order of these laws. Christ is 'our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, who made peace 'through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20, so that 'we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1. The escalation is that the peace offering celebrated a peace already made; Christ both makes the peace and becomes the feast. The type falls short because the meal was temporary and repeated; the peace of Christ is permanent.

typology.type: The blood that must not be eaten, Leviticus 7:26-27
typology.fulfillment: Israel was forbidden to eat blood because 'the life of the flesh is in the blood' and God had given it for atonement, Leviticus 17:11. Jesus reverses the prohibition at its deepest level: 'unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you,' John 6:53, and at the Supper He says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20. The life once reserved for the altar is now given to the believer. The type is a contrast, not a copy: what was forbidden in shadow is offered in reality.

typology.type: The priest's portion, the breast and the right thigh, Leviticus 7:31-34
typology.fulfillment: God took portions from the people's sacrifices and gave them to the priests as their living. Paul argues from this directly: 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings. In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel,' 1 Corinthians 9:13-14. The type falls short because the portions were fixed by law and tied to one family; in the church, provision for ministry is an act of shared love, Galatians 6:6.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ through the shape of the whole collection it closes. Leviticus 1 to 7 moves from sacrifices that deal with sin to a sacrifice that is a meal. In the priestly order of 6:8 to 7:38, the peace offering comes last, after the burnt, grain, sin and guilt offerings. Atonement comes first, fellowship follows. That is the order of the gospel. Christ is first the sin offering, Romans 8:3, and the guilt offering, Isaiah 53:10, and then the one who hosts His people at His table. 'Since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God,' Romans 5:1.

It leads to Christ through thanksgiving. The todah was the offering of a person who had been rescued. Psalm 116 is such a song: the psalmist was entangled by 'the ropes of death,' Psalm 116:3, and God delivered him, so he lifts 'the cup of salvation' and offers 'a sacrifice of thanksgiving,' Psalm 116:13 and 17. Jesus took bread and 'gave thanks,' Luke 22:19, on the night before His own death, and the church's central act of worship bears the name of thanksgiving. Those who share the Lord's Supper eat the peace offering of the rescued.

It leads to Christ through the blood. The law forbade Israel to eat blood because blood belonged to God for atonement. Jesus offers His blood to drink, John 6:53-56, not because the law was wrong but because the atonement it pointed to has been made. What the altar received, the believer now receives.

It leads to Christ through a warning. An unclean person who ate the peace offering was cut off, 7:20. Paul warns the Corinthians that whoever eats the Lord's Supper 'in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord,' 1 Corinthians 11:27. The table of the new covenant is freer than the old, but no less holy.

And it leads to Christ as both priest and portion. In Leviticus the priest received the breast and thigh from God. Christ is the priest who gives His own body: 'This is My body, given for you,' Luke 22:19. He is not supported by His people's offerings; He is Himself the food of His people.

These links need care. The breast and the thigh do not stand for Christ's love and strength, and the three kinds of cake do not represent the Trinity. The connections rest on the New Testament's own reading of the sacrificial meal, 1 Corinthians 10:16-18, and on the movement from sacrifice to fellowship that Leviticus 1 to 7 itself traces.
study.god:
This chapter shows God as a host. The peace offering is a meal where the worshiper eats before the LORD, and God is not a distant recipient but the giver of the feast. When Israel's elders went up Sinai, 'they saw Him, and they ate and drank,' Exodus 24:11. The peace offering carries that scene into ordinary life. God wants His people at His table.

It shows God as one who loves gratitude. Of all the reasons for a peace offering, the first named is thanksgiving, 7:12, and it has the strictest rule of time, eaten the same day. God does not want thanks postponed or hoarded. The psalms echo this: 'He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me,' Psalm 50:23.

It shows God as the Lord of life. The fat is His, and the blood is His, 7:23-27. These are not arbitrary bans but a teaching about ownership. Every animal killed for food, even at home, reminded Israel that life comes from God and returns to Him. This is why the command reaches back to Noah, Genesis 9:4. The God who gives life decides how it may be used.

It shows God's holiness guarding His generosity. The meal is freely given, but the unclean may not eat, and meat left too long becomes piggul. God's kindness is never casual. The feast is joyful because it is holy, not in spite of it.

It shows God as a provider who orders provision well. He takes the breast and thigh 'from the sons of Israel' and gives them 'to Aaron the priest and his sons as a permanent portion,' 7:34. The priests receive from God, not from their own grasping. When Eli's sons helped themselves, the LORD called it contempt, 1 Samuel 2:17. God's provision is generous, but it is His to give.

For worship, the chapter invites believers to thanksgiving that is prompt, shared and holy. Gratitude should be spoken while the mercy is fresh, in the company of others, with clean hands and a clean heart. The God who once invited Israel to feast before Him now invites His church to the table of His Son, and He is honoured when they come with thanks.

crossReferences.note: 'How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?' The psalmist answers with the offerings of Leviticus 7: he will lift 'the cup of salvation,' 'fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,' and 'offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving.' The thanksgiving and vow offerings of 7:12-16 here become public worship.

God says He does not need food, 'Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?' and then commands, 'Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.' The psalm keeps the todah and neder of Leviticus 7 but clarifies that they honour God, not feed Him.

'I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows.' The adulteress uses the same-day rule of Leviticus 7:15-16 as an invitation: she has meat that must be eaten now. It shows how a holy meal could be twisted into an occasion for sin, and how well the first readers knew these laws.

Eli's sons take meat with a fork before the fat is burned and demand raw meat by force. They violate exactly the order of Leviticus 7:30-34, where the fat is burned first and the priest receives only the breast and thigh God assigns. The narrator calls it contempt for the LORD's offering.

Gives the reason behind the ban of Leviticus 7:26-27: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar.' Blood is forbidden as food because it belongs to God as the means of atonement. The ban extends to the foreigner living in Israel.

The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain from blood and from the meat of strangled animals, echoing Leviticus 7:26-27 and 17:10-14. The decree shows the early church wrestling with how these laws bear on a mixed body of Jewish and Gentile believers sharing one table.

Paul argues from the priests' portions of Leviticus 7:31-36 that 'those who serve at the altar partake of its offerings,' and applies the principle: 'those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.' The breast and the thigh become a New Testament argument for supporting ministry.

Paul calls the cup and the bread 'a participation in the blood of Christ' and 'in the body of Christ,' and then points to Israel: 'Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?' The peace offering meal of Leviticus 7 is the Old Testament pattern for understanding the Lord's Supper as communion.

Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup 'in an unworthy manner' sins against the body and blood of the Lord. The warning echoes Leviticus 7:20-21, where the unclean person who eats the peace offering is cut off. The Lord's table, like the peace offering, joins joy with holiness.

Jesus says, 'unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you.' Against the background of Leviticus 7:26-27, where drinking blood meant being cut off, the saying was shocking. The life that belonged to God on the altar is now given to believers in Christ.

'Let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name,' and 'do not neglect to do good and to share with others.' The thanksgiving offering of Leviticus 7:12, which was shared with others, becomes the church's praise and generosity.

In a desolate Jerusalem God promises again 'the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD,' singing 'His loving devotion endures forever.' The todah of Leviticus 7 becomes a sign of restoration after exile, the sound of a people rescued and giving thanks.

study.oneStory:
In Eden humanity ate freely in God's presence, and every tree but one was given, Genesis 2:16. The fall turned that shared table into a place of shame and exile. Leviticus 1 to 7 traces the long way back, and this chapter ends it with a meal. After the burnt offering of surrender, the grain offering of dedication, and the sin and guilt offerings that deal with defilement and debt, comes the peace offering: God and His people eating together again.

The chapter answers what the earlier chapters left open. If sin can be atoned for, what is the goal? The goal is fellowship. The worshiper does not only walk away forgiven; he sits down to eat, with family, friends and priests, in the presence of the LORD. Yet the meal still carries the marks of a fallen world: the blood cannot be eaten, the meat spoils by the third day, the unclean are excluded.

It sets up what follows. The closing summary points ahead to the ordination of the priests in Leviticus 8, and the thanksgiving offering becomes the music of Israel's worship in the Psalms. After exile, Jeremiah hears the thank offerings return to Jerusalem, Jeremiah 33:11. Isaiah sees a greater feast, 'a banquet for all the peoples,' Isaiah 25:6, on God's mountain.

The story reaches its centre at the table where Jesus took bread and gave thanks. His body and blood are the true peace offering, and He made 'peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. The church eats this meal in thanksgiving, not once a year but whenever it gathers, proclaiming 'the Lord's death until He comes,' 1 Corinthians 11:26.

The story ends at another table. 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. There nothing will spoil, no one will be unclean, and the thanksgiving will never end. The peace offering of Leviticus 7, eaten in haste before morning, gives way to a feast in a city where there is no night, and the people of God eat and drink in His presence for ever.

quiz.q: How quickly must the meat of a thanksgiving peace offering be eaten?

options.text: On the same day it is offered; none may be left until morning.
options.note: Verse 15 explicitly requires this same day timing for the thanksgiving offering.

options.text: Within seven days.
options.note: The thanksgiving offering specifically requires same day consumption; a vow or freewill offering allows two days, not seven.

options.text: It may be kept indefinitely as long as it is refrigerated.
options.note: The text gives a strict same day requirement, with no allowance for extended storage.

options.text: No timing restriction is given.
options.note: Verse 15 gives an explicit, strict timing requirement.

quiz.q: What happens to meat from a peace offering that is eaten on the third day?

options.text: It is not accepted, will not be credited to the offerer, and is considered an abomination.
options.note: Verse 18 states this consequence explicitly for meat eaten on the third day.

options.text: It is considered especially holy and reserved for the high priest alone.
options.note: The text describes the opposite, that third day meat becomes unacceptable and defiling.

options.text: Nothing changes; it remains acceptable to eat at any time.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly states this meat becomes unacceptable after the permitted time.

options.text: No consequence is given.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly states the consequence.

quiz.q: What two things does this chapter permanently forbid Israel from eating?

options.text: Fat and blood.
options.note: Verses 23 to 27 establish this permanent prohibition against eating fat or blood of any bird or animal.

options.text: Bread and wine.
options.note: Bread and wine are not the subjects of this prohibition; fat and blood are.

options.text: Fish and honey.
options.note: The prohibition named in this chapter concerns fat and blood, not fish or honey.

options.text: Nothing is forbidden here.
options.note: Verses 23 to 27 give an explicit, permanent prohibition.

quiz.q: Which two portions of the peace offering are given permanently to Aaron and his sons?

options.text: The breast, as a wave offering, and the right thigh, as a contribution.
options.note: Verses 30 to 34 specify these exact portions as the priests' permanent share.

options.text: The entire animal, with nothing left for the worshiper.
options.note: The peace offering's meat is largely eaten by the worshiper; only the breast and thigh belong permanently to the priests.

options.text: The hide and the head only.
options.note: The hide belongs to the priest specifically for burnt offerings, verse 8; the peace offering's priestly portion is the breast and thigh.

options.text: No specific portion is given to the priests.
options.note: Verses 30 to 34 give a specific, detailed portion to the priests.

quiz.q: What does the chapter's closing summary, verses 37 to 38, list as the offerings given to Moses at Sinai?

options.text: The burnt offering, grain offering, sin offering, guilt offering, ordination offering, and peace offering.
options.note: Verse 37 lists exactly these six categories as a summary of the sacrificial law just given.

options.text: Only the burnt offering and the grain offering.
options.note: Verse 37 lists six distinct categories, not merely two.

options.text: The Ten Commandments.
options.note: This chapter's summary concerns the sacrificial offerings, not the Decalogue, which was given earlier in Exodus 20.

options.text: No summary is given.
options.note: Verses 37 to 38 give an explicit summary list.

questions: The thanksgiving offering had to be eaten the same day, shared quickly rather than hoarded. When God answers a specific prayer in your life, do you celebrate that promptly and share it with others, or do you let gratitude quietly fade?

The priests were given a rightful portion from the people's offerings so they would not go without. Do you support those who serve you spiritually, whether pastors, teachers, or leaders, as generously as this law required?
Fat and blood were permanently off limits, reserved wholly for God. What is the equivalent in your life, something you know belongs to God alone but you are tempted to keep or use for yourself?

Meat eaten past its proper time became an abomination rather than a blessing. Where might something good in your life, kept past its right season or used the wrong way, have turned from blessing into harm?
This chapter closes the entire sacrificial law given at Sinai. As you look back over these first offerings, which one has spoken most directly to where you are with God right now, and why?

translationNotes.note: Thanksgiving, todah, describes an offering brought in response to a specific deliverance or answered prayer, distinct from a general vow, neder, or freewill offering, nedavah, brought without a specific preceding occasion.

It shall be an abomination translates a strong Hebrew term, piggul, used specifically of sacrificial meat eaten past its permitted time, showing that even a holy offering could become defiling if handled wrongly.

The wave offering, tenufah, and the contribution, terumah, describe distinct ritual gestures, a horizontal waving and a lifting up, both marking the breast and thigh as formally set apart for the priesthood before being eaten.
